summary: The instructions add a gold-covered incense altar, a uniform half-shekel census payment, and a bronze basin for priestly washing. Special formulas for anointing oil and incense reserve them for sacred use, with explicit consequences for neglecting washing or reproducing the mixtures for unauthorized purposes.
whyItMatters: The sanctuary depends on recurring scent, water, money, and skilled preparation as well as its larger structure. Rules about shared payment and restricted substances distinguish communal support from private access to holy things.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: Moses' continuing Sinai instructions concerning sanctuary service, counting the people, and preparing sacred substances.
context.literaryForm: Several divine speeches prescribing an object, payment, washing, and restricted recipes with sanctions.

before.text: The priests' consecration and daily sacrifices have been described, ending in the promise that God will dwell among Israel. Further requirements now fill out how that service is sustained.

here.text: The chapter moves between an incense altar, counted persons, washed priests, and restricted mixtures, each with its own purpose and boundary.

after.text: God next appoints Bezalel and Oholiab with other skilled workers, reiterates Sabbath requirements, and gives Moses the covenant tablets.

outline.heading: The incense altar and its service
outline.note: The small gold-covered altar stands before the veil and receives daily incense and annual atonement.

outline.heading: A census ransom for sanctuary service
outline.note: Every counted man of the stated age gives the same half-shekel amount.

outline.heading: The washing basin
outline.note: Priests wash hands and feet before approach, under a warning of death.

outline.heading: The sacred anointing oil
outline.note: A specified mixture consecrates furnishings and priests and is forbidden for unauthorized reproduction or use.

outline.heading: The sacred incense
outline.note: Equal-weight spices are compounded and reserved for the meeting place, not personal scent.

keyVerses.text: The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel, when they give the offering of Yahweh, to make atonement for your souls.
keyVerses.why: The census payment is fixed equally for rich and poor among those counted.

keyVerses.text: When they go into the Tent of Meeting, they shall wash with water, that they don’t die; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn an offering made by fire to Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: The washing requirement is attached to a direct warning of death.

keyVerses.text: You shall not make this incense, according to its composition, for yourselves: it shall be to you holy for Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: The incense formula is expressly withheld from private reproduction and enjoyment.

questions.question: How is this altar different from the outer altar?
questions.answer: It is a smaller gold-covered acacia structure placed before the veil for sweet incense. Burnt, meal, and drink offerings are expressly excluded, so it has a distinct function even though it also has horns, rings, and carrying poles.

questions.question: When is incense burned and when is blood applied?
questions.answer: Aaron burns incense while tending the lamps each morning and evening. Once a year he makes atonement on the horns with blood from the sin offering of atonement, distinguishing the regular service from the annual act.

questions.question: What does “ransom” mean in the census instruction?
questions.answer: It is the required half-shekel payment each counted man gives for his life, with the stated aim of preventing a plague during the count. The money is then assigned to the Tent of Meeting's service as a memorial.

questions.question: Does equal payment mean this collection is voluntary?
questions.answer: No. The counted men aged twenty and upward are required to pay, with neither rich nor poor changing the amount. This fixed payment supports the tent’s service and functions as a memorial for those counted.

questions.question: Is the basin described only as a hygiene measure?
questions.answer: The priests must wash hands and feet before entering the tent or approaching the altar, and the command explicitly says so that they do not die. Washing belongs to the conditions for approaching the holy place and its service, with life and death at stake in the command.

questions.question: Why cannot the anointing oil be used as ordinary perfume?
questions.answer: Its named ingredients and quantities produce a mixture reserved to consecrate the sanctuary objects and priests. Reproducing it or putting it on an unauthorized person brings the stated penalty of being cut off, so the restriction is part of its assigned holy use.

questions.question: Does “cut off” specify exactly who carries out the penalty?
questions.answer: The oil and incense rules say the offender will be cut off from the people without describing an enforcement procedure in this chapter. The consequence is severe, but its precise mechanism is not explained here.

glossary.def: The fragrant mixture burned in regular sanctuary service and reserved from personal duplication.
The fixed payment measured by the sanctuary standard and required from each counted man.
The bronze water vessel between the tent and altar for washing the priests’ hands and feet.
